key_terms.meaning: Twisting effort at the crankshaft, in N·m; measured by a dynamometer and multiplied by speed to give power.
Usable power at the crankshaft: BP = 2πNT/60, with N in rev/min and T in N·m, answer in W.
Power developed on the pistons by the gas: IP = imep × V<sub>d</sub> × N/(60 n<sub>R</sub>) per cylinder, with imep in Pa, V<sub>d</sub> in m³ and N in rev/min (answer in W).
Power lost to friction, pumping and auxiliaries: FP = IP − BP.
Fraction of indicated power that reaches the shaft: η<sub>mech</sub> = BP/IP = 1 − FP/IP.
Fuel flow plotted against brake power at constant speed; extended to zero fuel it cuts the power axis at −FP.
Brake power divided by fuel energy rate: η<sub>bth</sub> = BP/(ṁ<sub>f</sub> × CV), with ṁ<sub>f</sub> in kg/s and CV in J/kg.
Indicated power divided by fuel energy rate: η<sub>ith</sub> = IP/(ṁ<sub>f</sub> × CV); η<sub>bth</sub> = η<sub>ith</sub> × η<sub>mech</sub>.
Fuel mass burned per unit of brake work: BSFC = ṁ<sub>f</sub>/BP, with ṁ<sub>f</sub> in kg/h and BP in kW, giving kg/kWh.
Ratio of actual air drawn per cycle to the theoretical swept volume of air at ambient density.
A fictitious constant pressure that would give the brake work in one cycle: bmep = 2π n<sub>R</sub> T / V<sub>d</sub>, with n<sub>R</sub> = 2 for a four-stroke and 1 for a two-stroke.
AFR = mass of air ÷ mass of fuel; equivalence ratio φ = (AFR)<sub>stoich</sub>/(AFR)<sub>actual</sub>, so φ > 1 is rich.
A running test on a multi-cylinder engine: cut one cylinder at a time and read the drop in brake power, which equals that cylinder's indicated power.
A loading device that absorbs engine torque and measures it, giving brake power directly when speed is known.
An account of fuel energy split into brake power, cooling water, exhaust gas and unaccounted losses, all in kJ/min or as percentages.
Heat released by burning unit mass of fuel completely, in kJ/kg; lower values about 44 000 kJ/kg for petrol and 42 500 kJ/kg for diesel.
A quartz sensor that turns in-cylinder pressure into a small electric charge for recording against crank angle.
Electronics that convert the tiny charge from a piezoelectric sensor into a proportional voltage for the data logger.
A shaft-mounted disc that gives one pulse per degree (or fraction) of rotation so pressure data can be tagged to crank position.
Rate at which chemical energy of the fuel appears as heat in the cylinder, computed from the pressure–crank-angle record.
A fixed speed–time schedule (for example MIDC or NEDC) that a vehicle follows on a chassis dynamometer so emission results are comparable.

takeaways: Every performance number is built from three measurements only: torque, speed and fuel flow.
Brake power is measured; indicated power is inferred; friction power is the difference between them.
A Morse test separates the cylinders' indicated powers by removing one working cylinder at a time.
Fuel flow and air flow must be logged with the load, because efficiency is meaningless without both.
A dynamometer is a calibrated brake; a test cell makes its reading repeatable and safe.
The heat balance sheet proves that the measured outputs add up to the fuel energy supplied.
Load, speed, AFR, ignition or injection timing, compression ratio and ambient conditions move power and efficiency together.
Performance improves through more air, better mixture, less friction, better control and cycle changes such as a higher compression ratio.
A result is valid only if the test standard, the running-in state and steady or transient condition are stated.
The in-cylinder pressure trace is the richest single record of what happens inside the engine.
bank_note: Long answers on engine testing are usually numeric plus explanatory: define the parameter with its formula and units, then substitute measured values and comment on whether the efficiency or the heat balance looks reasonable.

bank.q: Define brake power, indicated power and friction power, and derive the relation between them. Show how each is expressed in terms of torque, speed and mean effective pressure.
outline: BP = 2πNT/60 with symbols and units; measured by a dynamometer
IP from the indicator diagram: IP = imep × V<sub>d</sub> × N/(60 n<sub>R</sub>) per cylinder
FP = IP − BP and its parts (rubbing friction, pumping, auxiliaries)
η<sub>mech</sub> = BP/IP, typical values and why it falls at part load
All three in terms of mean effective pressure: fmep = imep − bmep; T = bmep × V<sub>d</sub>/(2π n<sub>R</sub>)
BP is measured, IP is inferred, FP is found by a separate test or by subtraction
answer: Brake power BP is the power delivered at the crankshaft, where the dynamometer (the "brake") measures it. One revolution turns the shaft through 2π radians, so with torque T in N·m and speed N in rev/min, BP = 2πNT/60 in W.

Indicated power IP is the rate at which the gas does work on the pistons. The area of the p-V loop is the work per cycle; dividing it by the swept volume V<sub>d</sub> gives the indicated mean effective pressure imep, so the work per cycle is imep × V<sub>d</sub>. A four-stroke completes one cycle in two revolutions (n<sub>R</sub> = 2), a two-stroke in one (n<sub>R</sub> = 1). Hence IP = imep × V<sub>d</sub> × N/(60 n<sub>R</sub>) per cylinder, multiplied by the number of cylinders.

Friction power FP is the part of IP that never reaches the shaft: FP = IP − BP. It has three parts: rubbing friction (piston rings and skirt, bearings, valve train), pumping work of the exhaust and intake strokes, and the drive of auxiliaries such as the oil pump, water pump and alternator.

Mechanical efficiency is the share that survives: η<sub>mech</sub> = BP/IP = 1 − FP/IP. It is about 0.80 to 0.90 at full load. FP changes little with load at fixed speed, so η<sub>mech</sub> falls at part load and is zero at idle, where all the indicated power goes on friction.

answer.text: Mean effective pressure form. Each power can be written with its own mean effective pressure: BP = bmep × V<sub>d</sub> × N/(60 n<sub>R</sub>), IP = imep × V<sub>d</sub> × N/(60 n<sub>R</sub>), FP = fmep × V<sub>d</sub> × N/(60 n<sub>R</sub>). Subtracting, fmep = imep − bmep. Equating BP = 2πNT/60 with the bmep form gives the torque relation:
answer.pre:
T = bmep × V<sub>d</sub> / (2π n<sub>R</sub>)      bmep = 2π n<sub>R</sub> T / V<sub>d</sub>
η<sub>mech</sub> = BP/IP = bmep/imep

answer.text: Numerical illustration (the single-cylinder four-stroke of the performance-parameters chapter: V<sub>d</sub> = 9.425 × 10⁻⁴ m³, 1500 rev/min, bmep 6 bar, η<sub>mech</sub> = 0.85):

answer: Which is measured: BP is measured directly from torque and speed, so it is the most reliable of the three. IP is inferred, from an indicator diagram or by a Morse test. FP is found by a separate test (motoring, Willans line) or by subtraction.
Check: η<sub>mech</sub> × IP = 0.85 × 8.32 = 7.07 kW = BP, and BP + FP = 7.07 + 1.25 = 8.32 kW = IP, so the three powers are consistent.

bank.q: Explain the Morse test for a four-cylinder engine. State its assumptions, the procedure, and how indicated and friction power are calculated.
outline: All cylinders firing at a set speed: note BP
Cut one cylinder, reduce the load to restore the same speed, note the new BP
The drop is the IP of the cut cylinder; repeat for every cylinder
Assumptions: FP unchanged, other cylinders unchanged, same speed
Total IP = sum of drops; FP = IP − BP; η<sub>mech</sub> = BP/IP
Limitations
answer: Principle: with all cylinders firing, BP = (IP of all cylinders) − FP. Cutting one cylinder removes its indicated power but leaves the friction of the engine. If the speed is restored, FP is the same, so the drop in BP equals the indicated power of the cut cylinder.

Set-up: a multi-cylinder engine (three or more cylinders) on a dynamometer, with a tachometer and a way to cut each cylinder: the spark plug lead of a petrol engine, or the fuel to one injector of a diesel.

answer.text: Procedure:
answer.pre:
1. Run the engine at the test speed and load until temperatures are steady; note BP (all firing).
2. Cut cylinder 1. The engine slows; reduce the dynamometer load until the speed is back
   at the test value. Note BP<sub>1</sub>.
3. Restore cylinder 1, let the reading settle, then cut cylinder 2 and repeat.
4. Do this for every cylinder, working quickly so temperatures do not change.

answer.text: Calculation: the indicated power of cylinder i is IP<sub>i</sub> = BP − BP<sub>i</sub>, and
answer.pre: IP = Σ (BP − BP<sub>i</sub>),   FP = IP − BP,   η<sub>mech</sub> = BP / IP

answer.text: Example with numbers (four-cylinder engine, BP = 20.0 kW all firing):

answer: Assumptions: (a) friction power is the same with a cylinder cut, which needs the same speed; (b) the firing cylinders give the same indicated power as before the cut; (c) the speed is brought back to the same value for every reading.

Limitations: it needs at least three cylinders; in a petrol engine with a shared intake manifold, cutting one cylinder changes the mixture and exhaust flow of the others; the cut cylinder still has pumping losses; small errors in each reading add up in the sum.
Check: the four drops are close to each other (5.7 to 6.0 kW), as they should be for identical cylinders, and FP comes out small and positive, so the readings are consistent.

bank.q: Describe the instruments used to measure fuel consumption and air consumption of an engine on a test bed, with the principle of each.
outline: Burette with three-way cock and stopwatch; density correction
Gravimetric method; rotameter, turbine and Coriolis meters
Air box with sharp-edged orifice and U-tube manometer, C<sub>d</sub> about 0.6
Viscous-flow meter and hot-wire meter
Both flows logged together with load and speed
answer: Why mass flow: combustion needs a fixed air mass per fuel mass, so both flows are wanted as mass flows, in kg/h or kg/s, logged at the same steady speed and load.

Burette (volumetric) method: the engine draws fuel from a glass burette between two marks of known volume V. A three-way cock lets the engine run from the tank while the burette fills, then switches it to the burette; a stopwatch times the fall between the marks. ṁ<sub>f</sub> = V × ρ × 3600 / t (V in L, ρ in kg/L, t in s, answer in kg/h). Example: 50 mL of diesel (0.83 kg/L) in 25 s gives 0.0415 × 3600 ÷ 25 = 5.98 kg/h.
Gravimetric method: the fuel tank stands on a balance and the time to use a fixed mass, say 100 g, is measured. No density is needed, so it is more accurate and is used to calibrate other meters.

Continuous fuel meters: a rotameter (a float rises in a tapered tube; needs density correction, steady flow only), a turbine meter (rotor speed gives volume flow as pulses) and a Coriolis meter (vibrating tube measures mass flow directly; the most accurate and the most costly).

answer.text: Air box with orifice: the engine breathes from a large box; air enters it through a sharp-edged orifice. The box damps the intake pulses so the orifice sees steady flow. A U-tube manometer reads the pressure drop as a water column h.
answer.pre:
Δp = 9.81 × h   (h in mm of water, Δp in Pa)
ṁ<sub>a</sub> = C<sub>d</sub> A √(2 ρ<sub>a</sub> Δp)   (C<sub>d</sub> ≈ 0.6 sharp-edged orifice)

answer: Other air meters: the viscous-flow (Alcock) meter passes the air through fine passages where the flow is laminar, so the pressure drop is proportional to flow and pulsations average correctly; a venturi has a higher C<sub>d</sub> (about 0.98) and a smaller permanent loss; a hot-wire or hot-film meter senses the cooling of a heated wire and responds fast enough for pulsating flow, which is why cars use it.

Using the two flows together: AFR = ṁ<sub>a</sub>/ṁ<sub>f</sub> (both in kg/s), and η<sub>vol</sub> = ṁ<sub>a</sub> ÷ (ρ<sub>a</sub> V<sub>s</sub> N/120) for a four-stroke. In the fuel-and-air chapter example, 0.052 kg/s of air with 1.66 × 10⁻³ kg/s of fuel gives AFR = 31.3 and η<sub>vol</sub> = 88.1 %.
Check: 31.3 is a sensible light-load diesel ratio, and 88.1 % lies in the normal 80 to 90 % band for a naturally aspirated engine, so the two instruments agree with each other.

bank.q: What is a heat balance sheet? List the items on the credit and debit sides and explain how each is evaluated from test data.
outline: Credit side: heat supplied = ṁ<sub>f</sub> × CV
Debit: brake power
Cooling water: ṁ<sub>w</sub> c<sub>pw</sub> ΔT<sub>w</sub>
Exhaust: (ṁ<sub>a</sub> + ṁ<sub>f</sub>) c<sub>pg</sub> ΔT<sub>g</sub>, or by an exhaust calorimeter
Unaccounted losses as the balancing term
Presentation in kJ/min (or kW) and per cent of heat supplied
answer: A heat balance sheet is an account of where the fuel energy goes during a steady engine test. The heat supplied by the fuel is the credit side; brake power, heat to the cooling water, heat carried by the exhaust and the unaccounted losses are the debit side. Both sides must be equal, and each debit is also given as a percentage of the heat supplied.
Credit, heat supplied: ṁ<sub>f</sub> × CV, with ṁ<sub>f</sub> from a burette or balance and CV the calorific value. In kJ/min: ṁ<sub>f</sub> (kg/min) × CV (kJ/kg).
Debit 1, brake power: from the dynamometer, BP = 2πNT/60; 1 kW = 60 kJ/min.

Debit 2, cooling water: ṁ<sub>w</sub> × c<sub>pw</sub> × (T<sub>out</sub> − T<sub>in</sub>), with ṁ<sub>w</sub> from a rotameter or a timed bucket, c<sub>pw</sub> = 4.18 kJ/(kg·K) and thermometers at the jacket inlet and outlet.

Debit 3, exhaust: ṁ<sub>g</sub> × c<sub>pg</sub> × (T<sub>g</sub> − T<sub>room</sub>), where ṁ<sub>g</sub> = ṁ<sub>a</sub> + ṁ<sub>f</sub> (air from the air box, fuel from the burette) and c<sub>pg</sub> is about 1.05 kJ/(kg·K). An exhaust gas calorimeter gives a check: heat to its water plus the heat still in the gas leaving it.

Debit 4, unaccounted: heat supplied minus the other three. It covers radiation and convection from the block, heat to the oil if not measured separately, and incomplete combustion. It is never measured.

answer.text: Example, presented in kJ/min (heat balance chapter engine: 3.0 kg/h of fuel at 42 MJ/kg, BP 10.5 kW, water 8 kg/min with 18 K rise, exhaust 93 kg/h with 400 K rise):

answer: Check: 630.0 + 601.9 + 651.0 + 217.1 = 2100.0 kJ/min and 30.0 + 28.7 + 31.0 + 10.3 = 100.0 %. The unaccounted term is positive and about a tenth of the heat supplied, which is the usual size; a negative value would show a mistake in units or in the exhaust mass flow.

bank.q: Explain the construction and working of absorption and eddy-current dynamometers. Why is a transient dynamometer needed for emission testing?
outline: Absorption types: Prony, rope, hydraulic, eddy-current
Torque from reaction arm and load cell: T = W × L
BP = 2πNT/60
Eddy-current: rotor in a magnetic field, no mechanical contact, load set by coil current, fast control, water cooled
Transient dynamometer: motors and absorbs, follows a driving cycle second by second
answer: An absorption dynamometer turns the engine's power into heat and measures the torque that does it. The types are the Prony brake and rope brake (friction), the hydraulic brake (water) and the eddy-current brake (electromagnetic).

Torque measurement: the absorbing element (brake block, water casing or eddy-current stator) is mounted so that it is free to turn, on trunnions. The engine tries to drag it round; an arm of length L holds it against a load cell or spring balance reading W. Torque T = W × L, and BP = 2πNT/60.

Hydraulic dynamometer: a rotor with vanes or cups turns inside a casing filled partly with water. The water is thrown outwards and drags on the casing; the water level sets the load. The water carries away the heat, so a continuous flow is supplied. It suits large powers at modest cost.

Eddy-current dynamometer construction: a toothed steel rotor on the engine shaft turns between the poles of field coils fed with direct current; the stator (casing) carries water passages. Working: as the teeth pass, the flux in the stator changes and induces eddy currents in it. These currents and the field oppose the motion, so the rotor is braked and the casing is dragged round; the arm and load cell read the torque. The heat from the eddy currents is removed by cooling water.

Features of the eddy-current type: no rubbing contact, so no wear and steady torque; the load is set by the coil current, so it can be changed quickly and smoothly and controlled electronically; it is compact. It can only absorb: it cannot drive the engine.

answer.text: Numerical example (hydraulic dynamometer of the dynamometers chapter):

answer: Why a transient dynamometer is needed for emission testing: emissions are certified over a driving cycle with rapid accelerations, decelerations, idling and engine braking. The dynamometer must change speed and torque second by second and must drive the engine during overrun. An AC dynamometer (a vector-controlled induction or synchronous machine of low inertia) works in all four quadrants, motoring and generating in both directions, so it can reproduce the cycle. Absorption dynamometers cannot motor the engine, and water and friction brakes respond too slowly.
Check: 9.42 kW at 60 N·m from a 1.0 L four-stroke gives bmep = 2π × 2 × 60 ÷ 10⁻³ = 7.54 bar, a normal value for a petrol engine at part load.

bank.q: List the engine operating variables that affect performance and state, for any four, the direction of their effect on power, efficiency and emissions.
outline: Speed, load, air-fuel ratio, ignition or injection timing
Compression ratio, valve timing, intake air temperature and density
Coolant and oil temperature, deposits and wear
Fuel quality, altitude and humidity
Direction of effect on power, efficiency and emissions for four variables, with reasons
answer: Variables: engine speed; load (throttle or fuel rack); air-fuel ratio (equivalence ratio φ); spark or injection timing; compression ratio; valve timing; intake air temperature, pressure and humidity (altitude and weather); coolant and oil temperature; deposits, wear and valve clearance; fuel quality (octane, cetane, calorific value, density); exhaust back pressure.

Speed: brake power rises with speed as more cycles run each second, then falls when breathing and friction losses grow. BSFC has a minimum at mid-speed, so brake thermal efficiency is highest there. Friction rises steeply at high speed.

Air-fuel ratio: maximum power at a slightly rich mixture (φ about 1.1), because all the air's oxygen is used; best efficiency at a slightly lean mixture (φ about 0.85 to 0.95), because the fuel burns completely, the gas has a higher ratio of specific heats and less heat is lost. Rich mixtures raise CO and HC; mixtures a little lean of stoichiometric give the most NOx; very lean mixtures misfire and raise HC.

Spark timing: MBT timing gives the most torque, with peak pressure about 15° after TDC. Advancing beyond it raises peak pressure, risks knock and raises NOx. Retarding lowers torque and efficiency, raises exhaust temperature and lowers NOx.

Intake air density: ρ = p/(RT). Hot or thin air means less air per stroke, so brake power falls roughly in proportion. Example: an engine giving 40 kW at 25 °C and 1.00 bar gives about 40 × 0.90 × 298/313 = 34.27 kW at 40 °C and 0.90 bar, a 14.3 % drop. Efficiency changes little; a diesel with fixed fuelling runs richer and smokes more.

Compression ratio: raising it raises indicated efficiency (Otto: 1 − 1/r<sup>0.4</sup>, 59.4 % at r = 9.5 against 61.7 % at r = 11), but in SI engines it is limited by knock and in diesels by peak pressure and NOx.

answer.text: Summary of directions:

answer: Check: in each case power follows the trapped air mass or the work extracted from it, and efficiency follows how completely and how early the fuel burns; this is why the curves move together.

bank.q: A four-stroke, four-cylinder engine has bore 80 mm, stroke 110 mm and runs at 3000 rpm. The measured brake torque is 120 N·m. Calculate brake power, swept volume per cylinder, and BMEP.
outline: Swept volume per cylinder = (π/4) × 0.080² × 0.110 = 5.529 × 10⁻⁴ m³
Total swept volume 2.212 × 10⁻³ m³; n<sub>R</sub> = 2 for a four-stroke
bmep = 2π n<sub>R</sub> T / V<sub>d</sub> = 6.82 bar
Check by BP = bmep × V<sub>d</sub> × N/(60 n<sub>R</sub>)
answer: Data: four cylinders, four-stroke (n<sub>R</sub> = 2), bore D = 0.080 m, stroke L = 0.110 m, N = 3000 rev/min, T = 120 N·m.

Method: brake power needs only torque and speed. bmep needs the total swept volume of all cylinders and the number of revolutions per cycle, n<sub>R</sub>, because bmep is the brake work per cycle divided by the swept volume. Work in SI units throughout: metres, N·m, rev/s, Pa.
Speed in rev/s: N = 3000 ÷ 60 = 50 rev/s. Angular speed ω = 2π × 50 = 314.16 rad/s, so BP = T × ω gives the same result as 2πNT/60.
Swept volume per cylinder: V<sub>s</sub> = (π/4) × D² × L = 0.7854 × 0.0064 × 0.110 = 5.529 × 10⁻⁴ m³ = 0.553 L.
Total swept volume: V<sub>d</sub> = 4 × 5.529 × 10⁻⁴ = 2.212 × 10⁻³ m³ = 2.21 L.

answer.text: bmep from torque:
bmep from power (second route):
answer.pre:
cycles per second = N/(60 n<sub>R</sub>) = 3000/120 = 25 s⁻¹
bmep = BP / (V<sub>d</sub> × 25) = 37 699 / (2.212 × 10⁻³ × 25) = 6.82 × 10⁵ Pa

answer.text: Results:

answer: Further quantities that follow: power per cylinder = 37.70 ÷ 4 = 9.42 kW; specific power = 37.70 kW ÷ 2.21 L = 17.0 kW per litre; brake work per cycle of the whole engine = bmep × V<sub>d</sub> = 6.82 × 10⁵ × 2.212 × 10⁻³ = 1508 J, which equals 2π n<sub>R</sub> T = 4π × 120 = 1508 J, the torque acting over the two revolutions of one cycle.
Mean piston speed, a useful sanity check: 2 × L × N/60 = 2 × 0.110 × 50 = 11.0 m/s, well inside the 8 to 15 m/s of road engines, so the speed and stroke are realistic.
Check: both routes give 6.82 bar, and 6.82 bar is a normal value for a naturally aspirated engine below peak torque. Using n<sub>R</sub> = 1 by mistake would give 3.41 bar, half the true value.

bank.q: An engine develops 40 kW brake power and consumes 11 kg of fuel per hour. The calorific value is 42 000 kJ/kg. Find brake thermal efficiency, BSFC, and the fuel energy rate in kW.
outline: Fuel energy rate = ṁ<sub>f</sub> × CV = 128.3 kW
BSFC = 11/40 = 0.275 kg/kWh
Comment for a CI engine
answer: Data: BP = 40 kW, fuel 11 kg/h, CV = 42 000 kJ/kg.

Definitions used: brake thermal efficiency is the brake power divided by the rate at which the fuel brings chemical energy in; BSFC is the fuel used per unit of brake work. Both must use the same time base, so convert kg/h to kg/s for the efficiency and keep kg/h for BSFC in kg/kWh.
Fuel mass flow: ṁ<sub>f</sub> = 11 ÷ 3600 = 3.056 × 10⁻³ kg/s.
Fuel energy rate: ṁ<sub>f</sub> × CV = 3.056 × 10⁻³ × 42 000 = 128.3 kJ/s = 128.3 kW.
Brake thermal efficiency: η<sub>bth</sub> = BP ÷ fuel energy rate = 40 ÷ 128.3 = 0.312 = 31.2 %.
BSFC: ṁ<sub>f</sub> ÷ BP = 11 kg/h ÷ 40 kW = 0.275 kg/kWh = 275 g/kWh.

answer.text: Second route for the efficiency, from BSFC:

answer: Comment: 31.2 % and 275 g/kWh are realistic for a small diesel at part load; a large diesel at its best point reaches about 200 g/kWh (about 43 %). The other 68.8 % of the fuel energy, 88.3 kW, leaves as heat to the coolant and exhaust and as friction.

answer.text: Summary:

answer: Sensitivity: if the fuel flow had been read as 12 kg/h, η<sub>bth</sub> would fall to 28.6 % and BSFC rise to 0.300 kg/kWh, so a 1 kg/h reading error moves the efficiency by about 2.6 percentage points; this is why the burette test is repeated and averaged.
Check: 40 + 88.3 = 128.3 kW, so the energy accounts close.

bank.q: In a Morse test on a four-cylinder engine running at constant speed, the brake power with all cylinders firing is 30 kW. Successive cut-outs give 21.6, 21.9, 21.7 and 21.5 kW. Find the indicated power of each cylinder, total IP, friction power and mechanical efficiency.
outline: Each IP = BP(all firing) − BP(that cylinder cut)
IP values 8.4, 8.1, 8.3, 8.5 kW
Total IP = 33.3 kW
η<sub>mech</sub> = 30/33.3 = 90.1 %; comment on the spread
answer: Principle: with the speed restored after each cut, friction power is unchanged, so the drop in brake power equals the indicated power of the cut cylinder: IP<sub>i</sub> = BP − BP<sub>i</sub>.

Procedure behind the numbers: the engine runs at a set speed with all four cylinders firing (30 kW). Cylinder 1 is cut, the engine slows, the dynamometer load is reduced until the speed is back at its set value, and the brake power is read (21.6 kW). The cylinder is restored and the step repeated for cylinders 2, 3 and 4.

answer.text: Indicated power of each cylinder:

answer: Total indicated power: IP = 8.4 + 8.1 + 8.3 + 8.5 = 33.3 kW.
Friction power: FP = IP − BP = 33.3 − 30.0 = 3.3 kW.
Mechanical efficiency: η<sub>mech</sub> = BP ÷ IP = 30.0 ÷ 33.3 = 0.901 = 90.1 %.
Comment: the four cylinders agree within 0.4 kW (about 5 %), so the cylinders are evenly loaded; cylinder 2 is slightly weak. A mechanical efficiency of 90 % is normal near full load.

Accuracy: each drop is a difference of two readings near 22 to 30 kW, so a 0.1 kW reading error is about 1 % of a cylinder's power; adding four such drops can shift IP by a few tenths of a kW, which changes FP by around 10 %. This is why the Morse test gives IP well but FP only roughly.

Indicated mean effective pressure follows if the swept volume is known; for example, with 0.5 L per cylinder at 3000 rev/min, imep = IP × 60 n<sub>R</sub> ÷ (V<sub>d</sub> × N) = 33 300 × 120 ÷ (2.0 × 10⁻³ × 3000) = 6.66 × 10⁵ Pa = 6.66 bar.

Assumptions to state in the answer: friction power is the same whether a cylinder fires or not; the firing cylinders deliver the same indicated power after the cut; the speed is the same for every reading. A negative or near-zero FP would show that one of these failed or a reading was copied wrongly.
Check: the average cylinder IP is 33.3 ÷ 4 = 8.33 kW, and BP + FP = 30.0 + 3.3 = 33.3 kW = IP.

bank.q: During a one-hour test an engine used 8 kg of fuel of calorific value 43 000 kJ/kg and produced 30 kW brake power. Cooling water flow was 15 kg/min with a 25 °C rise; exhaust gas flow was 4.0 kg/min with a 380 °C rise above room temperature and specific heat 1.05 kJ/(kg·K). Prepare the heat balance in kJ/min and in percent.
outline: Heat supplied = (8/60) × 43 000 = 5733.3 kJ/min
Brake power = 30 × 60 = 1800 kJ/min
Cooling water = 15 × 4.18 × 25 = 1567.5 kJ/min
Unaccounted = 769.8 kJ/min
Percentages and comment that the unaccounted term is positive and modest
answer: Method: draw up the sheet on a per-minute basis, because the water and exhaust flows are given per minute. Every term must be in kJ/min before adding: brake power in kW is multiplied by 60, and the fuel flow in kg/h is divided by 60.
Basis: one minute. Fuel used = 8 kg/h = 8/60 = 0.1333 kg/min.
Heat supplied: 0.1333 × 43 000 = 5733.3 kJ/min (that is 95.56 kW).
Heat to brake power: 30 kW = 30 kJ/s × 60 = 1800.0 kJ/min.
Heat to cooling water: ṁ<sub>w</sub> × c<sub>pw</sub> × ΔT<sub>w</sub> = 15 × 4.18 × 25 = 1567.5 kJ/min.
Heat to exhaust gas: ṁ<sub>g</sub> × c<sub>pg</sub> × ΔT<sub>g</sub> = 4.0 × 1.05 × 380 = 1596.0 kJ/min.

answer.text: Heat balance sheet:

answer: Brake thermal efficiency: 31.4 %, and BSFC = 8 ÷ 30 = 0.267 kg/kWh.

Consistency of the data: the exhaust flow is 4.0 × 60 = 240 kg/h, so the air flow is 240 − 8 = 232 kg/h and the air-fuel ratio is 29, a normal diesel value. (An exhaust flow far larger than air plus fuel would make the unaccounted term negative.)

Comment: brake power, cooling water and exhaust each take between a quarter and a third of the fuel energy, the usual pattern for a diesel. The unaccounted 13.4 % is positive and modest; it covers radiation and convection from the hot block, heat to the oil and incomplete combustion.

answer.text: The sheet drawn as one bar of heat supplied (lengths to scale):

svg.aria: Bar of 5733 kJ per minute split into brake power 31.4 per cent, cooling water 27.3, exhaust 27.8 and unaccounted 13.4 per cent.
svg.body: <rect x="40.0" y="40" width="200.9" height="44" rx="3" style="fill:var(--live-soft);stroke:var(--live);stroke-width:2"/><text x="140.4" y="68" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle" style="fill:var(--ink)" font-weight="700">31.4 %</text><text x="140.4" y="30" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle" style="fill:var(--ink)">Brake power</text><text x="140.4" y="106" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle" style="fill:var(--muted)">1800.0</text><rect x="240.9" y="40" width="175.0" height="44" rx="3" style="fill:var(--accent-soft);stroke:var(--accent);stroke-width:2"/><text x="328.4" y="68" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle" style="fill:var(--ink)" font-weight="700">27.3 %</text><text x="328.4" y="30" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle" style="fill:var(--ink)">Cooling water</text><text x="328.4" y="106" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle" style="fill:var(--muted)">1567.5</text><rect x="415.9" y="40" width="178.2" height="44" rx="3" style="fill:var(--next-soft);stroke:var(--next);stroke-width:2"/><text x="505.0" y="68" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle" style="fill:var(--ink)" font-weight="700">27.8 %</text><text x="505.0" y="30" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle" style="fill:var(--ink)">Exhaust gas</text><text x="505.0" y="106" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle" style="fill:var(--muted)">1596.0</text><rect x="594.1" y="40" width="85.9" height="44" rx="3" style="fill:var(--panel);stroke:var(--line2);stroke-width:2"/><text x="637.1" y="68" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle" style="fill:var(--ink)" font-weight="700">13.4 %</text><text x="637.1" y="30" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle" style="fill:var(--ink)">Rest</text><text x="637.1" y="106" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle" style="fill:var(--muted)">769.8</text><text x="360" y="136" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle" style="fill:var(--muted)">kJ/min; total 5733.3 kJ/min of heat supplied</text>

answer: Why each term is evaluated as it is: the cooling water term uses the rise in water temperature, not its outlet temperature; the exhaust term uses the rise above room temperature, because the air entered at room temperature; the brake term is work, so it is counted at its full value; the remainder cannot be measured and is found by difference.
Check: 1800.0 + 1567.5 + 1596.0 + 769.8 = 5733.3 kJ/min, equal to the heat supplied.

bank.q: A sharp-edged orifice of 40 mm diameter in an air box passes air when the head across it is 60 mm of water. Ambient air density is 1.2 kg/m³ and the coefficient of discharge is 0.62. Find the air mass flow rate, and the volumetric efficiency of a 1.5 litre four-stroke engine running at 2500 rpm if it consumes this air.
outline: Ideal velocity √(2Δp/ρ) = 31.32 m/s
ṁ<sub>a</sub> = C<sub>d</sub> × A × v × ρ = 0.02928 kg/s
Theoretical air = ρ × V<sub>s</sub> × N/(60 × 2) = 0.0375 kg/s for a four-stroke
η<sub>vol</sub> = 78.1 %
answer: Set-up: the engine draws all its air from a large air box; air enters the box through the sharp-edged orifice. The box damps the pulses of the intake strokes, so the flow through the orifice is steady and the orifice equation applies. A U-tube manometer across the orifice reads the pressure drop as a column of water.
Orifice area: A = (π/4) × 0.040² = 1.2566 × 10⁻³ m².
Pressure drop: a 60 mm water column gives Δp = ρ<sub>w</sub> g h = 1000 × 9.81 × 0.060 = 588.6 Pa.
Ideal air velocity through the orifice: v = √(2Δp/ρ<sub>a</sub>) = √(2 × 588.6 ÷ 1.2) = √981 = 31.32 m/s.

answer.text: Air mass flow:
Theoretical air flow of the engine (four-stroke: one intake stroke per two revolutions):

answer: Volumetric efficiency: η<sub>vol</sub> = 0.02928 ÷ 0.0375 = 0.781 = 78.1 %.

Why C<sub>d</sub>: the jet leaving a sharp-edged orifice contracts (the vena contracta) and loses a little energy to friction, so the real flow is only about 0.6 of the ideal; C<sub>d</sub> = 0.62 corrects for both.

Meaning of the result: the engine traps 78.1 % of the air its swept volume could hold at room density. The losses come from the pressure drop across the air filter, throttle and inlet valve, from heating of the charge by hot walls, and from residual exhaust gas in the cylinder.

Check: 78.1 % is a little below the usual 80 to 90 % for a naturally aspirated engine at full throttle, which suits part throttle or a restrictive intake. Forgetting the ÷ 2 for a four-stroke would give 39.0 %, an impossible value that flags the mistake.

bank.q: Indicated power cannot be measured directly on a production engine. Compare the precision, assumptions and limitations of the Morse test, the motoring test and the use of a cylinder pressure transducer for obtaining IP.
outline: Morse test: running engine, assumes FP and the other cylinders unchanged, sensitive to speed control
Motoring test: gives friction (so IP = BP + FP); no combustion, cooler parts, no gas load on rings
Pressure transducer: direct p-V integration, needs TDC referencing and pegging
Comparison of accuracy, cost, time and applicability
Recommendation by purpose
answer: All three methods aim at IP. The Morse test gives IP directly as a sum of brake-power drops; the motoring test gives FP, and IP = BP + FP; the cylinder-pressure transducer gives IP from the p-V loop. Willans line is a fourth route, like the motoring test giving FP.

Morse test: assumptions are that friction is unchanged when a cylinder is cut, that the other cylinders keep their indicated power and that speed is restored. Precision: IP is a sum of differences, so small reading errors add (in a four-cylinder test, a 0.1 kW error per reading can move FP by around 10 %). Limits: three or more cylinders; in a petrol engine the cut cylinder upsets mixture and exhaust flow of the others. Cost and time: only a dynamometer, a few minutes.

Motoring test: the engine is driven without fuel by a motoring dynamometer at the test speed, just after a firing run so it is warm; the power needed is FP. Assumption: friction without combustion equals friction when firing. Limits: no gas pressure behind the rings (lower ring friction), cooler cylinder and oil (higher viscous friction), different pumping work; the errors partly cancel but not reliably. It needs an electric dynamometer that can motor.

Cylinder-pressure transducer: a piezoelectric sensor and crank-angle encoder record p against θ for 100 or more cycles; imep is the closed-cycle integral ∮p dV ÷ V<sub>d</sub>. Requirements: accurate TDC (a one-degree error changes imep noticeably), pegging to absolute pressure, a cooled flush-mounted sensor and a data system. It gives IP cylinder by cylinder and cycle by cycle, plus peak pressure, heat release and COV of imep.

answer.text: Comparison:

head: Feature
Morse test
Motoring test
Pressure transducer
rows: any, one cylinder at a time

answer: Evaluation with numbers: in the Morse test example (four cylinders, BP 30 kW, IP 33.3 kW) FP is 3.3 kW; a pressure-transducer measurement on the same engine would give IP directly, and any difference between the two indicates the Morse assumption errors. For the friction-measuring chapter's diesel, Willans line gave FP = 3.75 kW at 1500 rpm.

Recommendation: for development work and combustion research, the pressure transducer, because it is the only method that sees the real firing cycle; for a routine check of a multi-cylinder engine in a teaching lab or workshop, the Morse test, because it is quick and cheap; the motoring test where friction itself is studied part by part (strip-down tests), accepting its bias.
Check: whichever method is used, the result must satisfy IP > BP with η<sub>mech</sub> in a sensible band (about 0.75 to 0.92 at full load); a value outside it points to a measurement error.

bank.q: Evaluate the methods available to improve engine performance and rank them by their effect on brake thermal efficiency and emissions.
outline: Four levers: more air, better mixture, less friction, better control
Turbocharging and intercooling for trapped air mass
Injection pressure, spray and direct injection
Friction reduction
Control: VVT, electronic timing, closed-loop AFR, cylinder deactivation
Cycle changes: compression ratio, Miller/Atkinson
Trade-off with NOx and particulates
Justified ranking
answer: Basis for ranking: brake thermal efficiency η<sub>bth</sub> = η<sub>ith</sub> × η<sub>mech</sub>, so a method helps by raising indicated efficiency (more work from the same heat) or mechanical efficiency (less friction), or by letting a smaller engine do the same job at a better load point. Emissions are judged on NOx, particulates, CO and HC.

More air (turbocharging with intercooling): raises trapped air mass, so power rises roughly with density. Example: density × 1.4 on an 80 kW engine gives 112 kW at the same BSFC of 240 g/kWh. Its efficiency gain comes mainly from downsizing: a smaller engine runs at higher load, where friction is a smaller share. Emissions: higher temperatures raise NOx; intercooling limits it.

Higher compression ratio and Miller/Atkinson timing: raise indicated efficiency directly. Example: r from 9.5 to 11 raises the Otto efficiency from 59.4 % to 61.7 %, a factor of 1.039. Limited by knock (SI) and peak pressure (CI). Miller timing lowers charge temperature, helping knock and NOx, but needs boost to keep power.

Better mixture (high-pressure common rail, direct injection, swirl and tumble): faster, more complete burning raises indicated efficiency and lowers smoke and HC; advancing injection raises NOx, so it is traded against after-treatment.

Less friction (low-viscosity oil, low-tension rings, coatings, variable oil pump): raises mechanical efficiency with no emission penalty. Example: cutting FP from 12 kW to 10.2 kW adds 1.8 kW of brake power for the same fuel. Limited by wear at high load.

Better control (closed-loop lambda, knock sensing, electronic timing, VVT, cylinder deactivation, stop-start): keeps the engine at its best point across the map, cuts pumping loss at part load and enables three-way catalysts (large emission benefit).

answer.text: Ranking (for a road vehicle engine):

head: Rank
Method
Effect on η<sub>bth</sub>
Effect on emissions
rows: small (3 % of BP in the example)

answer: Justification: control ranks first because it improves efficiency and emissions together at every operating point. Boosting ranks next because the downsizing it allows gives the largest real-world fuel saving, but it must be managed for NOx. Cycle changes give a sure thermodynamic gain but are capped by knock. Friction work is the cheapest and safest, but each step is small.

Check with the combined example: compression ratio 11 plus 15 % less friction lift brake power from 60 kW to 64.61 kW at the same fuel, a 7.7 % rise in power and a 7.1 % fall in BSFC (60 ÷ 64.61 = 0.929); the gains add because one acts on indicated power and the other on friction.

bank.q: Discuss why an emission or power figure is meaningless unless the test standard, driving cycle and running-in condition are stated. Include the difference between gross and net power and between steady-state and transient testing.
outline: Agreed procedure: ambient correction, fuel, auxiliaries fitted
Gross power (essential auxiliaries only) against net power (as installed)
Running-in: friction falls and power settles
Correction to reference air with an example
Steady-state test cells against transient tests on driving cycles
Driving cycles: MIDC, NEDC, WLTC; cycle-to-cycle variation and logging
answer: A measured power or emission depends on how the test was run as much as on the engine. A standard fixes the procedure so that two laboratories get the same answer: what is fitted to the engine, how long it was run in, the speeds, the fuel, the air conditions and the correction to reference air, and for emissions the driving cycle.

Gross and net power: gross power is measured on a bare engine with only the auxiliaries it needs to run; net power is measured with the production fan, alternator, air cleaner and exhaust system fitted, as installed. The fan, alternator and silencer each take power, so the same engine can be rated, say, 60 kW gross and 52 kW net. ISO 1585 and SAE J1349 define net power for road vehicles; ISO 3046 covers industrial and marine engines; IS 10000 gives the Indian test methods for stationary engines.
Running-in: a new engine's rings and bearings bed in over the first hours, so friction falls and power rises; the standard fixes how long and at what load the engine runs before measurement.

answer.text: Reference air: power depends on air density, so a standard corrects the measured power to 25 °C and 99 kPa dry pressure. For a spark-ignition engine:

answer: The same engine therefore has an observed 52.0 kW and a corrected 55.0 kW, 6 % apart; quoting one without saying which is meaningless. The correction is applied only while α stays between 0.93 and 1.07.

Steady-state and transient testing: a steady-state test holds speed and load until readings stop drifting, good for maps of BSFC and power. Emissions in real use come from transients: accelerations, cold start, gear changes. Transient tests use an AC dynamometer (engine) or a chassis dynamometer (vehicle) that follows a speed-time schedule second by second.

answer.text: Driving cycles decide the emission number:

head: Cycle
Duration
Distance
Character
rows: BS VI cars and light vehicles

answer: A CO figure in g/km from NEDC cannot be compared with one from WLTC, because the speed and load history differ. Limits such as BS VI petrol car CO of 1.0 g/km have meaning only on the cycle they are written for.

Data validity: in-cylinder results such as imep need 100 or more cycles because of cycle-to-cycle variation; a COV of imep of 2.56 % (0.21 bar on 8.2 bar) is stable, but a single cycle could be several per cent off the mean.

Conclusion: a valid figure states the standard (gross or net, ISO 1585 or SAE J1349), the running-in, observed or corrected air, the fuel, steady or transient, and for emissions the cycle. Check: in the example the correction alone moved the power by 3.0 kW, larger than many design improvements, which shows why the procedure must be stated.

glossary.def: A dynamometer that converts the absorbed engine power into heat, as in water-brake and eddy-current types.
A large settling chamber fitted with an orifice or nozzle, used to measure the air drawn by an engine smoothly and steadily.
Brake mean effective pressure, the constant pressure that would produce the measured brake work in one cycle.
Brake specific fuel consumption, the fuel mass needed per kilowatt-hour of brake work.
The Indian Bharat Stage VI emission norm, applied to new vehicles from 2020, with tight limits on NOx, particulate matter and sulphur in fuel.
An electronic unit that converts the charge from a piezoelectric sensor into a proportional voltage.
The scatter in pressure and work between successive cycles of the same cylinder under identical settings, usually given as the COV of imep.
A dynamometer that loads the engine by electromagnetic drag with no mechanical contact, allowing fast control.
Power measured with only the auxiliaries essential for running; net power is measured with the full installation.
The rate of chemical energy release during combustion, calculated from the cylinder pressure trace.
A statement showing how the fuel energy supplied is divided between brake power, cooling, exhaust and unaccounted losses.
The Modified Indian Driving Cycle, the speed–time schedule used in India for chassis dynamometer emission tests.
A test in which an external motor drives the engine without fuel to measure its friction and pumping losses.
The New European Driving Cycle, a speed–time schedule for vehicle emission testing consisting of urban and extra-urban phases.
The simplest absorption dynamometer, using friction on a drum and a measured reaction arm.
The initial period of engine operation in which surfaces bed in, friction falls and performance stabilises.
A test condition in which speed, load and temperatures are held constant for long enough for all readings to settle.
The minimum air mass per unit fuel mass needed for complete combustion; about 14.7 for petrol and 14.5 for diesel.
A controlled room with a dynamometer, cooling, ventilation, fuel supply and instrumentation for repeatable engine testing.
The ratio of the air actually trapped per cycle to the swept volume of air at ambient conditions.
A straight line of fuel flow against brake power at constant speed, extended to zero fuel flow to estimate friction power.
A dynamometer in the drive line that measures torque as the power passes through, from shaft twist or strain gauges, absorbing almost none of it.
Shifting a relative piezoelectric pressure record by a constant so that it reads absolute pressure.
The multiplier that converts power measured in test-cell air to power at the standard's reference air conditions.
Actual fuel-air ratio divided by the stoichiometric fuel-air ratio; above 1 is rich, below 1 is lean.
Standard deviation of imep over many cycles divided by the mean imep, in per cent; a measure of combustion stability.
